title: ack-driven-splitting-and-scheduler-effects-on-streaming-latency-nov-2026
body:
Summary:
We ran a set of micro and end-to-end experiments to isolate how ack-driven packet/split behavior from edge proxies interacts with client-side request schedulers and server KV cache warmup. The focus: quantify tail and median latency regressions that appear when proxies emit split frames on client ACK windows and when client schedulers re-coalesce or re-order writes. This doc collects motivation, test harness, raw observations, and suggested mitigations for the serving-runtime and edge-proxy teams.

Motivation / background:
- Production incidents in Oct-Nov 2026 showed intermittent 95th/99th latency spikes in hosted inference with small incremental tokens and heavy KV cache churn.
- Hypothesis: intermediate proxies that split outgoing frames for MTU/pacing reasons create small fragments that interact poorly with client scheduler heuristics (Nagle-ish coalescing, flush timing), causing extra kernel wakeups and de-synchronized KV cache warmup (more misses).
- Goal: measure the contributions from proxy-side splitting, client flush timing, and server-side scheduling to end-to-end QoS.

Test harness overview:
- Cluster: 4-worker cluster (r4-large-gpu-equivalent), single-edge-proxy VM (envoy-like) + serving runtime process. Measurements collected with pprof/goroutine dumps, kernel tcp_info, and custom tracer that timestamps at: client-write, proxy-ingest, proxy-egress, server-receive, server-token-emit, client-receive.
- Workloads: three synthetic workloads:
  1) small-step-chat: 1–3 tokens per flush, 15–30ms think time between user keystrokes (simulating typing streams)
  2) batch-inference: larger single chunk payloads (2–8k tokens) to stress throughput path
  3) mixed-burst: alternating small-step-chat bursts with occasional large messages (reflects UI+background tasks)
- Transports: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 (h2) streaming, gRPC server-streaming over HTTP/2.
- Client schedulers: a) aggressive coalesce (flush every 2–3ms), b) conservative coalesce (flush every 20ms), c) ack-aware scheduler that defers flush until ack from server.

Metrics captured:
- median / p50, p95, p99 end-to-end latency (client write => client receive first token)
- server CPU cycles and GPU stall time (coarse)
- KV cache miss rate per request
- kernel-level syscalls per request (send/recv counts)
- proxy buffer fragmentation count (number of chunks emitted per logical request)

Key observations (condensed):
1) Proxy-induced splitting increases p95 by 12–40ms for small-step-chat when client uses aggressive coalescing. The worst case had proxy emit 3 fragments for a single small token; each fragment caused an additional epoll wakeup in the server process.
2) Conservative client coalescing (20ms) improved median latency slightly for small-step-chat (p50 -6ms) but increased tail (p99 +10ms) in mixed-burst due to head-of-line blocking when large messages pre-empt small ones on the same connection.
3) Ack-aware scheduler reduced p99 by up to 22ms for HTTP/2 streaming in the presence of proxy-splitting because it synchronized client flushes with server-driven ACKs, avoiding unnecessary small-fragment bursts.
4) gRPC server-streaming showed more resilience to split fragmentation than raw HTTP/1.1 chunked because gRPC uses larger initial frames and protobuf framing masks tiny-chunk amplification. However, when the proxy re-packetized to smaller sizes (simulated MTU trimming), gRPC p95 regressed ~8ms.
5) KV cache miss amplification: when first fragment arrived significantly earlier than subsequent fragments (fragment spacing > 4ms), server started token processing with incomplete KV context leading to extra lookups and ~1.7x miss rate on first token. This correlated with higher CPU time on the CPU-side of the runtime.
6) Syscall churn: aggressive coalesce + proxy splitting produced ~2.2x more send syscalls per logical request vs ack-aware scheduler.

Representative numbers (small-step-chat workload, median across 1000 requests):
- baseline (no proxy split, conservative client): p50=18ms, p95=52ms, p99=78ms
- proxy split + aggressive client: p50=20ms, p95=84ms, p99=130ms
- proxy split + ack-aware client: p50=19ms, p95=62ms, p99=96ms

Interpretation / root causes:
- Fragmentation amplifies kernel wakeups and scheduling noise in the server process; this is a dominant contributor to observed tail latency in small-token streaming cases.
- Client-side schedulers matter: naive aggressive flushers increase syscall churn and expose the server to microburst arrivals; conservative flushers help median but can worsen tail due to queuing behind large requests.
- Synchronization (ack-aware behavior) provides the best tradeoff in our tests for streaming UX workloads because it aligns the client emission with server processing windows and KV cache readiness.
- Proxy behavior matters: proxies that re-chunk without preserving original logical message boundaries cause the worst amplification.

Actionable mitigations (short-term -> long-term):
- Short term (runtime/client): publish a recommended SDK scheduler setting for streaming clients (default: ack-aware flush with 4ms grace window). Update SDK docs and experimental client flag. (owner: devx)
- Mid term (proxy config): add an envoy filter to avoid re-splitting frames below a 512B threshold for streaming endpoints; add a flag to preserve logical-message boundaries for routes tagged as streaming. (owner: infra/proxy)
- Mid term (runtime): add lightweight token-level arrival coalescing in the runtime ingest pipeline to treat closely spaced fragments (<5ms gap) as a single logical arrival for KV warmup. (owner: serving-runtime)
- Long term (scheduling): evaluate kernel-bypass techniques or shared memory passthrough on high-throughput nodes to reduce epoll wakeups on fragment-heavy paths. (owner: infra/experimental)

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What's the impact on cost (CPU cycles) for ack-aware scheduling at larger scale (100k rps)? Need a throughput-focused sweep.
- How do mobile networks with variable RTT interact with ack-driven heuristics? Do we see increased reordering on cellular? (cc: solutions-eng)
- Can we detect proxy re-chunking in the trace pipeline and automatically apply server-side coalescing heuristics per-request?

Notes / tactical experiment ideas to run next:
- Re-run mixed-burst at 50k rps with ack-aware client and measure total CPU cost and GPU utilization.
- Add a variant where proxy uses a 1ms pacing rule (simulates rate-limiter smoothing) and measure effect on p99.
- Synthetic test where fragments are intentionally interleaved (simulate multiplexed flows) to test ingestion hedging logic.

Appendix: brief instrumentation checklist
- ensure tracer timestamps are monotonic and include kernel-level tcp_info (snd_mss, rtt, unacked)
- attach pprof heap/cpu before/after major run; collect eBPF syscall histograms for sendmsg/sendto counts
- add connection-level fragment histogram to existing telemetry (metric: proxy.fragment_count_by_conn, tag: route)

Owner / next steps:
- Priya Singh (owner) to open follow-up spike: SRV-1245-run1 to validate coalescing change on dev cluster by 2026-12-10.
- Ethan Martinez to prototype envoy filter (PR draft linked in artifacts)

If reviewers want the raw traces and the R notebooks that produced the latency CDFs, see linked_artifacts or ping me directly. This is a working doc — comments welcome on the mitigation prioritization and whether to pursue kernel-level experiments early.
